performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How do trills and tiny repeated notes turn a costume design into music?
intro: Children in eggshell costumes dance in a ballet: a quick scherzino, a trio of chirping trills, then the scherzino again without the trio. Listen for the trills. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

cues.title: Woodwinds, harps, plucked strings
cues.text: Ravel uses a delicate palette here: woodwinds, harps and pizzicato strings, with bright percussion. Detected attacks run at about five a second at a quiet level near −20 dB, as small as the dancers.
cues.evidence: Onsets per second 5.2, 5.2, 5.8 at 0:00–0:10; relative level −19.9 to −17.9 dB. Woodwinds, harps, pizzicato strings and percussion: Philharmonia guide; the report does not identify instruments.

cues.title: The trio: trills and tremors
cues.text: At about 0:34 the trio begins. In the piano score it is built on trills and quickly rocking pairs of notes, which an orchestra can turn into chirps. Detected attacks fall at first, to 2.6 a second, while the sound brightens.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 0:34 (novelty 0.86); onsets per second 4.6 (0:30), 2.6 (0:35); brightness 1,378 Hz (0:35) rising to 2,075 Hz at 0:55. The trio and its trills are in Lamm’s piano score (Mutopia, ballet.ly); the orchestral scoring is not checked against a score.

cues.title: Canaries in armour
cues.text: Hartmann’s costume design for Petipa’s ballet Trilby, given in St Petersburg in 1871, shows canary chicks in eggshells; Stasov wrote of canaries “enclosed in eggs as in suits of armor”. It is the picture on the Hartmann edge.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition) for Trilby, Petipa and Gerber, the 1871 date and Stasov’s description; the sketch itself is the art of the site’s edge hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874 (File:Hartmann Chicks sketch for Trilby ballet.jpg).

cues.title: Back to the scherzino
cues.text: The strongest boundary of the movement, at 1:02, brings the scherzino back. The score says to repeat it without the trio, then add a coda. Detected attacks reach their highest rate, over six a second, just before the return.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:02 (novelty 1.00); onsets per second 6.2 at 1:00, 5.2 at 1:05; relative level −18.7 dB (1:00). “De Capo il Scherzino, senza Trio, e poi Coda” is the instruction in Lamm’s score (Mutopia).

transitions.title: Staccato gives way to trills
transitions.how: The staccato chatter of the scherzino stops and the trio takes over. In the piano score its figures are trills and pairs of notes rocking quickly back and forth; scored for the orchestra they brighten the sound while reducing the number of separate attacks. The pulse stays quick, so the join is a change of texture, not tempo.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:34 (novelty 0.86); onsets per second 4.6 (0:30) to 2.6 (0:35); brightness 1,310 Hz (0:30) rising to 2,075 Hz (0:55). The trio’s trills are in Lamm’s piano score; the orchestral treatment is not checked against a score.

transitions.title: The trio ends and the opening returns
transitions.how: Attacks multiply again, up to more than six a second, and at about 1:02 the scherzino of the opening returns word for word. The score’s direction is da capo senza trio, so the trio is not repeated. Because the same music comes back, the movement closes the circle and the earlier chirping is heard in a new light.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:02 (novelty 1.00); onsets per second 5.0 (0:50), 6.2 (1:00), 5.2 (1:05). Da capo senza trio: Lamm’s score (Mutopia, ballet.ly). The recurrence is not matched by the report’s self-similarity, so only the score instruction is claimed.

transitions.title: A few loud chords close it
transitions.how: The scherzino’s chatter ends and a short extension finishes the piece with a few louder chords: detected attacks drop from over five a second to under two, and the level climbs from −16.5 dB to −11.1 dB, one of the loudest windows of the movement. The coda adds no new idea; it cuts the dance off, as a curtain falls on a ballet scene.
transitions.evidence: Relative level −16.5 dB (1:10) to −11.1 dB (1:15, second of the movement’s loudest windows after 0:55 at −10.9 dB); onsets per second 5.4 (1:10) to 1.6 (1:15). A terse coda follows the da capo in the score instruction and in Wikipedia’s description.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (1:20; this file is 1:18), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
